tagline: A marsh channel and a former ferry port frame the shore.
intro: On Virginia’s Eastern Shore, Route 13 divides the peninsula into bayside and seaside areas. Route 180 crosses between them, passing through Pungoteague and Keller before reaching Wachapreague’s waterfront in the Atlantic-side wetlands. At Wachapreague, the channel continues through marshes toward the barrier islands.

At the peninsula’s southern end, Kiptopeke served as the northern landing for ferries across the lower Chesapeake Bay. The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel replaced that service in 1964. The former terminal later became a campground, then a state park in 1992.

For the drive to Wachapreague, Route 180 runs east from Pungoteague to Keller, briefly joins US 13 north, then turns east across an inactive railroad line. Wachapreague Road becomes Main Street, ending at Atlantic Avenue beside the channel.

moments.title: Onancock
moments.text: A Virginia highway marker dates Onancock’s founding to 1680. In the mid-19th century, the town was a stagecoach stop between Wilmington, Delaware, and Eastville. Its creek had also brought a call for military aid: on November 28, 1782, Commodore Zedechiah Whaley sailed upstream and appealed to Lieutenant Colonel John Cropper. Cropper gathered 25 local men, who boarded Whaley’s flagship, Protector, to join the campaign against British barges. In the Battle of Kedges Strait, Protector fought on after three other barges withdrew; 25 of its 65 men were killed or wounded.

moments.title: Wachapreague
moments.text: The road ends before the water route does. Route 180 reaches Atlantic Avenue on Wachapreague’s waterfront. Beyond town, Wachapreague Channel winds through seaside marsh and reaches the Atlantic between Cedar and Parramore islands. Access to both marsh and ocean draws fishermen here. The town’s name comes from the Wachapreague, an Algonquian people who lived in the area centuries ago.
moments.notice: Wachapreague Channel winds from the waterfront into the seaside marsh.

moments.title: Kiptopeke State Park
moments.text: At Kiptopeke, concrete ships were sunk to protect the former ferry port from erosion during severe storms. The ferry service ended in 1964 when the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel took over the crossing. John Maddox later bought the terminal and operated a campground before selling the property to the state in 1992. The terminal building became an education and concessions building, but was razed by 2002. The park’s shoreline, beach and piers give access to the Chesapeake Bay’s brackish water. The shoreline also provides migratory bird habitat along the East Coast flyway, another role for land once used to move motorists across the bay.
moments.notice: Concrete ships mark the former ferry port.
